card.summary: 'Please, fill in this form to get your FREE IPv6 tunnel.' The form asks for an email and 'IPv4 address of your side of the tunnel'.

free_tier.stated: 'Please, fill in this form to get your FREE IPv6 tunnel.' The form asks for an email and 'IPv4 address of your side of the tunnel'.
free_tier.notes: Each user of the tunnel broker is provided with an own IPv6 network of size /48.

egress.terms: 'We provide our service free of charge.' No traffic allowance, rate or fair-use clause is published.; ingress: udp

record.interface_detail: a web form for registration and an HTTP auto-update URL for a dynamic endpoint address
record.tooling: unknown until the protocol is known; iproute2 for a 6in4 tunnel, wg-quick if WireGuard exists
record.chaining: would compose with a free VM the same way Route64 does, if the protocol turns out to be routable
record.limits_note: A public IPv4 address is required at the user's end of the tunnel.
record.binding_note: No quota, rate or object cap is published, so nothing in the vocabulary fails at 1 TiB/month. What is unproven is whether the tunnel can carry the traffic at all, which is a protocol question rather than a limit.

identity_cost.detail: 'E-mail (will be your login)'. No card, phone or national identity is asked for. The vendor warns against hotmail and live.com addresses because mail to them is blocked.

record.reliability_note: mail to hotmail and live.com addresses is blocked by the mail provider, so a password may never arrive; support is one address and a phone number in Kyiv.
record.confidence_note: The free tunnel and the IPv4 endpoint shape are documented. The protocol, the prefix size and whether WireGuard is offered at all were not established: reading the FAQ and help paths returned 404, and the account pages need a login. One vendor sentence naming the tunnel type and prefix would raise this to documented.

evidence.proved: free registration, the auto-update endpoint for a dynamic IPv4, and 'We provide our service free of charge.'

egress.terms: No traffic allowance is published in available documentation; ingress: tcp+udp

record.interface_detail: 'The broker's website contains a large number of different configurations for various operating systems and equipment.'
record.tooling: iproute2 or any 6in4-capable router; the site publishes per-OS configurations
record.chaining: pairs with any free VM that has a public IPv4, since 6in4 needs one; it is the cheapest way to give such a VM a routed /48.
record.binding_note: Nothing in the vocabulary is stated: the /48 is free, no byte meter is published and no rate is published. The gate is a capability rather than a quota: 'To work the tunnel, you need to have a public ("honest") IPv4 address', so a client behind CGNAT cannot use it at all. Reachability is IPv6-only.

identity_cost.detail: https://tb.netassist.ua/ offers 'register a new user (it's FREE!)'; the login page warns 'Please, do NOT use hotmail and live.com mail accounts! They've baned us for some unknown reasons'.

record.reliability_note: single country, single PoP; the operator states that hotmail and live.com mail domains are blocked on its side.
record.confidence_note: the /48, the price and the public-IPv4 requirement are documented from the vendor page; the transport protocol is only named by the handwiki broker list, not by NetAssist, and that third-party statement is what holds the record at reported. A vendor page naming 6in4 or GRE, or a provisioned tunnel, would raise it.

record.notes: One PoP (Kiev), operating since 2011, page footer says 2011-2026. A BGP-enabled tunnel is available by email for clients with their own AS and address space. The company sells /48 PI space plus an ASN for EUR 300/year, which is a separate product from the free broker. The site is a 2011-era broker with an email login, an IPv4 endpoint field and a dynamic-IP updater, which is the classic protocol-41 shape described in the Wikipedia tunnel broker article; that is inference, not evidence.
